# Maṅgala Sutta (Snp 2.4 (PTS Snp 46))
**ID:** Snp 2.4 (PTS Snp 46)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Maṅgala Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp2.4
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Maṅgala Sutta* (also known as the *Mahāmaṅgala Sutta*) is the fourth discourse of the Cūḷavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Winternitz 1933]. Introduced by a prose preface in which an inquiring deity requests the Buddha to explain what constitutes the highest blessing (*maṅgala*), the text consists of twelve verses outlining a progressive path of skillful conduct and social virtues [SuttaCentral; Powers 2016; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. These blessings range from everyday social and domestic foundations—such as avoiding fools, associating with the wise, revering parents, caring for spouse and children, blameless livelihoods, and abstaining from intoxicants—to emotional stability in the face of worldly conditions (*phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi*) and the realization of *nibbāna* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism].
Celebrated as one of the most widely recited discourses in the Theravāda world, the sutta holds a preeminent place in the *paritta* (protective chant) collection [Powers 2016; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. It long formed an essential curricular text for early monastic and lay literacy, notably in Burma where it was memorized by young students [Turner 2009]. In sixteenth-century Chiang Mai, the scholar-monk Sirimaṅgala composed the *Maṅgalatthadīpanī*, a monumental Pali commentary on the sutta that greatly expanded on obligations to parents and the practice of giving (*dāna*); this commentary remains a central fixture of monastic education in Thailand [von Hinüber 1996; Heim 2004; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism].
Within the Pali canon, the text is duplicated in its entirety as the fifth discourse of the *Khuddakapāṭha* (Kp 5) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2018]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive textual reuse between Snp 2.4 and Kp 5 (§0.1–13.5) with a similarity score of 0.98, alongside shared opening and framing verses in the *Devaputta Saṁyutta* (SN 2), *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1), and *Parābhava Sutta* (Snp 1.6), and extensive citations in the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* and *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, SuttaCentral records a Chinese parallel in chapter 39 of the *Fa ju piyu jing* (T 211.39) [SuttaCentral]. A Tibetan Kangyur translation titled the *Mahāmaṅgala-sūtra* (D0043) was executed with the Sinhalese scholar-monk Ānandaśrī, corroborating DharmaNexus cross-language alignments with D0043, the *Svastigāthā* (D4400), and the *Devaparipṛcchāmaṅgalagāthā* (D1100) [Gaffney 2003; DharmaNexus].
